To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the recognition heuristic is used adaptively across domains, but not in line with individual cue validity differences between domains.

(1) people adaptively change their reliance on recognition across domains, (2) this change is not related to the validity of recognition in a domain, (3) people have metacognitive awareness of the domain differences, (4) this metacognitive awareness is not related to recognition validities in a domain.
people are sensitive to the usefulness of recognition memory in a domain and adaptively change their reliance on it between domains.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how humans exploit recognition as a cue for judgments.
the question of whether people can adaptively use recognition as a frugal strategy.

the question of how people can adapt to differences in recognition memory between domains and provides new insight into the interplay of strategic, intra-individual and environmental, inter-individual processes in judgment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
people have metacognitive knowledge about the global differences between task domain, but no access to the validity of the recognition cue in each domain.

people have metacognitive awareness of the usefulness of recognition as a cue for judgment across task domains, but that this awareness is not fine-grained enough to be used for adaptive changes in the use of recognition.
people have a general, intuitive notion of the usefulness of recognition, but not of its validity, across different domains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

people have a metacognitive sense of the utility of recognition, which is not necessarily based on a detailed understanding of individual cue validities, but which is sufficient for strategic, adaptive changes in the use of recognition.
people are sensitive to global differences in recognition validity, but not to the individual recognition validites.
the RH can be a useful heuristic, but only if people are sensitive to the environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people are sensitive to the general usefulness of recognition in decision making and adaptively change their reliance on it across task domains.
people are sensitive to the usefulness of recognition in different task domains.
people adapt their decision strategies to differences in task environments in a flexible and adaptive manner.
